hook.text: Chat apps update instantly. Stock tickers stream live. HTTP's request-response pattern can't do that alone.

buildup.text: WebSocket starts as an HTTP request, then upgrades to a full-duplex, persistent connection.

discovery.text: Once open, either side can send messages at any time. No polling, no waiting, just real-time data flow.

twist.text: WebSocket connections stay open for minutes or hours. That's great for users but costly for servers at scale.

climax.text: Slack, Discord, live sports — any app with instant updates likely uses WebSockets or something similar.

punchline.text: WebSocket keeps the line open so data flows freely.

quiz.question: How does WebSocket differ from standard HTTP?
options: It maintains a persistent two-way connection
It uses a completely different port than HTTP
It encrypts data without needing TLS

details.summary: WebSocket provides a persistent, full-duplex communication channel over a single TCP connection between a browser and server.
details.whyItMatters: WebSocket makes real-time web applications possible. Without it, features like live chat, stock tickers, and collaborative editing would require inefficient polling techniques.
takeaways: WebSocket enables two-way communication over a single connection
An HTTP upgrade handshake initiates the persistent connection
Messages flow in both directions without request-response overhead

faq.question: How does WebSocket differ from regular HTTP?
faq.answer: HTTP is request-response: the client asks, the server answers. WebSocket allows both sides to send messages independently at any time over a persistent connection. There is no need for the client to repeatedly poll the server. This reduces latency and bandwidth for real-time applications.

faq.question: When should you use WebSocket vs Server-Sent Events?
faq.answer: Use WebSocket when both client and server need to send data in real time, like chat or gaming. Use Server-Sent Events when only the server pushes updates to the client, like news feeds or dashboards. SSE is simpler, auto-reconnects, and works over standard HTTP.
